questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Trigonometric Functions With Linear Arguments
questions.worked_solution:
If we let $u=2x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi /4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\pi /2$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}9\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}9\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}(0-1) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

If we let $u=\frac{\pi x}{4},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\pi }{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{4}{\pi }\,\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\pi /2$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{4})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{4}{\pi }\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }(1-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
If we let $u=\frac{x}{4},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $2\pi /3$ | $2\pi $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\pi /6$ | $\pi /2$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{2\pi }\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{csc}⁡(u)\operatorname{cot}⁡(u)\cdot 4\,\text{d}u \\  & =4{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{csc}⁡(u)\operatorname{cot}⁡(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =4(-\operatorname{csc}⁡(u))\,{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2} \\  & =4(-\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})) \\  & =4(-1+2) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Products Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
Let $u=2{x}^{2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{\pi }$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $2\pi $ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{x}^{2})\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡u{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}(1-1) \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Quotients Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
If we let $u={sin}^{2}⁡(x)+3,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,⟹\,\text{d}u=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi /2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $3$ | $4$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}{{sin}^{2}⁡(x)+3}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡(x)+3}\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|\,{|}_{3}^{4} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
If we let $u=8{cos}^{3}⁡(x)+5,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8{cos}^{3}⁡(x)+5)=-24{cos}^{2}⁡(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).
$$

So, differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-24{cos}^{2}⁡(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=24\operatorname{sin}⁡(x){cos}^{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\pi /3$ | $\pi /2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $6$ | $5$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{24\operatorname{sin}⁡(x){cos}^{2}⁡(x)}{8{cos}^{3}⁡(x)+5}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{8{cos}^{3}⁡(x)+5}\cdot 24\operatorname{sin}⁡(x){cos}^{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{6}^{5}\frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\text{d}u) \\  & =-{\int }_{6}^{5}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{6}^{5} \\  & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡5-\operatorname{ln}⁡6) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{6}{5})\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}))=2y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}).
$$

So, let $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}).$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=2y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u=y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})\,\text{d}y.
$$

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})}{\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})}\,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})}\cdot (y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}))\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})|+C\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If we let $u=\dfrac x 3,$ then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac 1 3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x =3\, \textrm d u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{3})\,\text{d}x & =2\int \operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\cdot 3\int \operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡u+C \\  & =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+C\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $u = x^3 - \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 3x^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 3 \textrm d u = x^2\,\textrm d x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}x & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(u)\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {sec}^{2}⁡(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})+C\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Integrating Quotients Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution
canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate the integral $\displaystyle \int_0^{\pi/4} \dfrac{\tan x \sec^2 x}{1+\tan^2x}\,\textrm d x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(1+\tan^2 x) = 2\tan{x}\sec^2 x.
$$

So, let $u = 1+\tan^2 x.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 2\tan x\sec^2 x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u = \tan x\sec^2 x\,\textrm d x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi/4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$
